questions.questionText: Which organelle is the main site of aerobic respiration in a eukaryotic cell?
questions.explanation: The mitochondrial matrix and inner membrane contain the pathways that generate most ATP during aerobic respiration.

curriculum.subskill: Identify the site of aerobic respiration
curriculum.objective: Interpret cell structures and membrane transport processes to explain movement, compartmentalisation and cellular function.

questions.questionText: A plant cell is placed in a solution with a lower water potential than the cell sap. What is the immediate net movement?
options: Water leaves the cell by osmosis
Solute leaves through the cell wall only
questions.correctAnswer: Water leaves the cell by osmosis
questions.explanation: Water moves down its water-potential gradient across the partially permeable membrane, from the cell to the external solution.

curriculum.objective: Interpret cell structures and membrane transport processes to explain movement, compartmentalisation and cellular function.

questions.questionText: Why does facilitated diffusion stop increasing at very high solute concentration?
options: All available transport proteins become occupied
questions.correctAnswer: All available transport proteins become occupied
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion depends on a finite number of carrier or channel proteins, so transport reaches a maximum when they are saturated.

curriculum.objective: Interpret cell structures and membrane transport processes to explain movement, compartmentalisation and cellular function.

questions.questionText: A toxin prevents ATP production. Which membrane process is most directly reduced before concentration gradients collapse?
options: Pumping sodium ions against their gradient
questions.correctAnswer: Pumping sodium ions against their gradient
questions.explanation: Moving sodium against its electrochemical gradient is active transport and directly requires ATP, unlike the passive processes listed.

curriculum.objective: Interpret cell structures and membrane transport processes to explain movement, compartmentalisation and cellular function.

questions.questionText: Which monomers join to form a protein?
questions.explanation: Proteins are polypeptides formed when amino acids join through peptide bonds in condensation reactions.

curriculum.objective: Relate molecular structure to biological function and analyse factors that affect enzyme-controlled reactions.

questions.questionText: Why are phospholipids well suited to forming cell membranes?
options: They have hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails
They contain enzymes in their tails
questions.correctAnswer: They have hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails
questions.explanation: Their amphipathic structure causes a bilayer to form in water, with heads facing water and tails sheltered inside.

curriculum.objective: Relate molecular structure to biological function and analyse factors that affect enzyme-controlled reactions.

questions.questionText: An enzyme’s rate rises from 20°C to 40°C but falls sharply at 70°C. What best explains the fall?
options: The active site loses its complementary shape
The enzyme gains additional peptide bonds
questions.correctAnswer: The active site loses its complementary shape
questions.explanation: High temperature disrupts bonds maintaining tertiary structure, denaturing the enzyme and altering its active site.

curriculum.objective: Relate molecular structure to biological function and analyse factors that affect enzyme-controlled reactions.

questions.questionText: A competitive inhibitor is added to an enzyme reaction. Which change can most effectively reduce the inhibitor’s effect?
questions.explanation: More substrate molecules compete for active sites, increasing the chance that substrate rather than inhibitor binds to the enzyme.

curriculum.objective: Relate molecular structure to biological function and analyse factors that affect enzyme-controlled reactions.

questions.questionText: During which stage of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?
questions.explanation: DNA synthesis occurs during S phase so each chromosome has two sister chromatids before cell division.

curriculum.objective: Use genetic information and cell-division principles to predict inheritance, variation and chromosome behaviour.

questions.questionText: Two heterozygous parents, Aa × Aa, have a child. What is the probability of genotype aa?
questions.explanation: The cross produces AA, Aa, Aa and aa in equal combinations, so one of four expected genotypes is aa.

curriculum.objective: Use genetic information and cell-division principles to predict inheritance, variation and chromosome behaviour.

questions.questionText: Which process during meiosis directly creates new combinations of alleles on homologous chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Non-sister chromatids exchange corresponding DNA segments during prophase I, producing recombinant allele combinations.

curriculum.objective: Use genetic information and cell-division principles to predict inheritance, variation and chromosome behaviour.

questions.questionText: A diploid cell has 12 chromosomes before DNA replication. How many chromosomes and chromatids are present at metaphase of mitosis?
questions.explanation: Replication doubles chromatids, not chromosome number; each of the 12 chromosomes consists of two sister chromatids at metaphase.

curriculum.objective: Use genetic information and cell-division principles to predict inheritance, variation and chromosome behaviour.

questions.questionText: Which feature of alveoli most directly shortens the diffusion distance for gases?
questions.explanation: A thin epithelial barrier creates a short path between alveolar air and blood, increasing the rate of diffusion.

curriculum.objective: Explain how specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems maintain efficient movement of substances in organisms.

questions.questionText: What is the main force moving water upward through xylem in a transpiring plant?
options: Tension generated by evaporation from leaf surfaces
questions.correctAnswer: Tension generated by evaporation from leaf surfaces
questions.explanation: Evaporation lowers leaf water potential and creates tension that pulls the cohesive water column upward through xylem.

curriculum.objective: Explain how specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems maintain efficient movement of substances in organisms.

questions.questionText: Why is the left ventricular wall thicker than the right ventricular wall?
options: It receives blood directly from veins
It generates higher pressure for systemic circulation
questions.correctAnswer: It generates higher pressure for systemic circulation
questions.explanation: The left ventricle must drive blood around the entire body, requiring more muscle and higher pressure than the pulmonary circuit.

curriculum.objective: Explain how specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems maintain efficient movement of substances in organisms.

questions.questionText: During vigorous exercise, which combination promotes oxygen unloading from haemoglobin in active muscle?
options: Lower carbon dioxide and higher pH
Lower temperature and lower carbon dioxide
Higher carbon dioxide and lower pH
questions.correctAnswer: Higher carbon dioxide and lower pH
questions.explanation: Active tissues produce carbon dioxide and acid; the resulting Bohr effect lowers haemoglobin affinity and promotes oxygen release.

curriculum.objective: Explain how specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems maintain efficient movement of substances in organisms.

questions.questionText: What term describes all the populations of different species living and interacting in one area?
questions.explanation: A community consists of the populations of different species that live and interact within the same area.

curriculum.objective: Analyse ecological evidence and selection pressures to explain population change, biodiversity and evolutionary outcomes.

questions.questionText: Why does antibiotic resistance become more common in a bacterial population after repeated antibiotic use?
options: Antibiotics teach every bacterium to resist
Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce more successfully
All susceptible bacteria mutate in the same way
questions.correctAnswer: Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce more successfully
questions.explanation: The antibiotic creates selection pressure: resistant variants leave more descendants, increasing resistance alleles in the population.

curriculum.objective: Analyse ecological evidence and selection pressures to explain population change, biodiversity and evolutionary outcomes.

questions.questionText: A mark–release–recapture study marks 40 beetles. Later, 50 beetles are caught and 10 are marked. What population estimate is obtained?
questions.explanation: The estimate is first sample × second sample ÷ marked recaptures: 40 × 50 ÷ 10 = 200 beetles.

curriculum.objective: Analyse ecological evidence and selection pressures to explain population change, biodiversity and evolutionary outcomes.

questions.questionText: A predator is removed from a food web. Its herbivore prey increases rapidly, then declines below its original level. Which explanation best fits the pattern?
options: Predator removal immediately increased plant biomass
Herbivores stopped reproducing because predation ended
The prey overshot carrying capacity and depleted its food resource
questions.correctAnswer: The prey overshot carrying capacity and depleted its food resource
questions.explanation: Release from predation can cause rapid growth, but resource depletion then increases competition and mortality, producing a population crash.

curriculum.objective: Analyse ecological evidence and selection pressures to explain population change, biodiversity and evolutionary outcomes.
